q: In Myanmar, copper and lead are rich mineral resources, and iron is a fairly rich resource.
e: Myanmar has abundant deposits of copper and lead, along with fairly rich iron ore resources.

q: Iron ore deposits in Myanmar are commonly found in Southern Shan State and Kayin State.
e: Iron ore deposits in Myanmar are commonly found in Northern Shan State and in Kachin State.

q: Copper deposits in Myanmar start from the lower Chindwin area through Sabe Taung, Kyesin Taung, Letpadaung Taung, Monywa, and Kawlin area.
e: These locations represent the major copper deposit regions extending through the northern part of Myanmar.

q: If a metal is less reactive than carbon, it can be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon as a reducing agent.
e: Carbon can reduce the oxides of metals that are below it in the reactivity series.

q: Aluminium ore is bauxite, which is treated with sodium hydroxide to obtain pure alumina.
e: Bauxite is processed with sodium hydroxide to remove impurities and yield pure aluminium oxide (alumina).

q: Molten cryolite is added to dissolve alumina because it has a higher melting point than alumina.
e: Molten cryolite is added because it has a lower melting point than alumina, which reduces the temperature of fusion.

q: In the extraction of aluminium, aluminium is produced at the anode and oxygen is liberated at the cathode.
e: In the extraction of aluminium, aluminium is produced at the cathode and oxygen is liberated at the anode.

q: Aluminium is a silvery-white metal that is very ductile and malleable.
e: These are the characteristic physical properties of pure aluminium.

q: The melting point of aluminium is 660°C.
e: Aluminium has a relatively low melting point of 660°C compared to transition metals.

q: In moist air, a film of oxide is formed on the aluminium surface which prevents any further attack on the underlying metal.
e: This protective aluminium oxide layer is chemically inert and prevents corrosion.

q: Aluminium reacts rapidly with dilute sulphuric acid to give aluminium sulphate and oxygen gas.
e: Aluminium reacts slowly with dilute sulphuric acid to give aluminium sulphate and hydrogen gas.

q: When aluminium is exposed to hot concentrated sulphuric acid, the result is aluminium sulphate, water, and sulphur dioxide.
e: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid acts as an oxidizing agent, producing sulphur dioxide gas.

q: Both dilute and concentrated nitric acids react very rapidly with aluminium.
e: Both dilute and concentrated nitric acids react very slowly with aluminium due to the protective oxide layer.

q: Aluminium reacts with alkalis, making it an amphoteric metal.
e: Aluminium is amphoteric because it can react with both acids and alkalis.

q: The reduction of a metallic oxide with aluminium is known as the Thermite reaction.
e: The Thermite reaction uses aluminium as a reducing agent to extract metals like iron from their oxides, releasing a lot of heat.

q: Haematite ($Fe_2O_3$) and magnetite ($Fe_3O_4$) ores are suitable for the extraction of iron.
e: These are the primary iron ores used in the blast furnace for iron extraction.

q: In the blast furnace, coke burns to produce carbon monoxide directly from oxygen.
e: In the blast furnace, coke burns to produce carbon dioxide, which then reacts with more carbon to form carbon monoxide.

q: Carbon monoxide reduces the oxides of iron to iron in the blast furnace.
e: Carbon monoxide is the primary reducing agent that converts iron oxides to molten iron.

q: Limestone breaks down due to the heat of the furnace to form calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
e: Calcium carbonate decomposes thermally to form calcium oxide, which acts as a basic flux.

q: Calcium oxide reacts with sand (silicon dioxide) to form calcium silicate, which is known as slag.
e: Calcium silicate ($CaSiO_3$) is the slag that floats on molten iron and is removed.

q: The iron obtained from the blast furnace is known as pig or cast iron and contains about 4% carbon.
e: Pig iron is the crude iron product from the blast furnace, containing approximately 4% carbon and other impurities.

q: Wrought iron is the impurest form of industrial iron.
e: Wrought iron is the purest form of industrial iron, obtained by removing impurities from pig iron.

q: Pure iron is soft, malleable, and rusts easily in damp air.
e: Unlike its alloys, pure iron is relatively soft and highly susceptible to rusting.

q: Unlike most other metals, pure iron is magnetic.
e: Iron is one of the few elements that exhibit strong ferromagnetism at room temperature.

q: The melting point of pure iron is 1538°C.
e: Pure iron has a high melting point of 1538°C.

q: When chlorine passes over heated iron, iron is oxidised to iron(II) chloride.
e: When chlorine passes over heated iron, iron is oxidised to iron(III) chloride.

q: When a mixture of iron filings and sulphur powder is heated, black iron(II) sulphide is formed.
e: Iron reacts with sulphur upon heating to form black iron(II) sulphide ($FeS$).

q: Iron reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form iron(III) sulphate and hydrogen gas.
e: Iron reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form iron(II) sulphate and hydrogen gas.

q: With hot concentrated sulphuric acid, iron gives iron(III) sulphate, water, and sulphur dioxide.
e: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid oxidizes iron to the +3 oxidation state, producing sulphur dioxide.

q: Iron reacts with hydrochloric acid to form iron(II) chloride and hydrogen gas because the production of hydrogen gas prevents further oxidation of $Fe^{2+}$ to $Fe^{3+}$.
e: The hydrogen gas produced acts as a reducing environment, keeping iron in the +2 oxidation state.

q: The lead ore, galena ($PbS$), is ground into small particles and put through a flotation process.
e: Galena is concentrated using the froth flotation process before extraction.

q: In the extraction of lead, the powder is heated to more than 1370°C, producing lead(II) oxide and volatile sulphur dioxide.
e: This roasting step converts lead(II) sulphide to lead(II) oxide.

q: The resulting lead(II) oxide is further heated in a blast furnace with oxygen to produce molten lead.
e: The resulting lead(II) oxide is further heated in a blast furnace with carbon to produce molten lead.

q: At the refining stage, lead is about 95% pure and is further refined to get greater than 99% purity.
e: Initial reduction yields ~95% pure lead, which is then refined by melting and skimming to exceed 99% purity.

q: Lead is a bluish-grey metal and is the softest of the metals in common use.
e: Lead is very soft and can be easily pressed into any form.

q: Lead is a good conductor of electricity and heat.
e: Lead is a poor conductor of electricity and heat compared to other common metals.

q: On exposure to air, lead is tarnished owing to the formation of a layer of hydroxide and carbonate.
e: This protective layer prevents further attack on the underlying lead metal.

q: The melting point of lead is 328°C.
e: Lead has a relatively low melting point of 328°C.

q: Lead does not react with water or steam.
e: Lead is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not react with water or steam.

q: Dilute sulphuric acid has a vigorous action upon lead to form lead(II) sulphate and hydrogen gas.
e: Dilute sulphuric acid has no appreciable action upon lead due to the formation of an insoluble lead(II) sulphate layer.

q: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with lead to form lead(II) sulphate, water, and sulphur dioxide.
e: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid acts as an oxidizing agent, reacting with lead to produce sulphur dioxide.

q: Lead reacts with dilute nitric acid to form lead(II) nitrate, water, and nitrogen oxide.
e: Dilute nitric acid oxidizes lead, producing nitrogen oxide ($NO$) gas.

q: Lead reacts with hot concentrated nitric acid to form lead(II) nitrate, water, and nitrogen dioxide.
e: Concentrated nitric acid is a stronger oxidizing agent, producing nitrogen dioxide ($NO_2$) gas.

q: The main source of copper ore is copper pyrites, also known as chalcopyrite ($CuFeS_2$).
e: Chalcopyrite is the most abundant and economically important copper ore.

q: Copper ore typically contains a high percentage of copper and does not need to be concentrated.
e: Copper ore typically contains a low percentage of copper and has to be concentrated before refining.

q: In the extraction of copper, the concentrated ore is heated strongly with silicon dioxide and air or oxygen in a furnace.
e: This smelting process converts the ore into copper(I) sulphide and removes iron as slag.

q: The copper in copper pyrites is reduced to copper(II) sulphide.
e: The copper in copper pyrites is reduced to copper(I) sulphide ($Cu_2S$).

q: The iron in copper pyrites is converted into an iron(II) silicate slag which is removed.
e: Iron reacts with silicon dioxide to form iron(II) silicate slag ($FeSiO_3$), which is separated.

q: Most of the sulphur in copper pyrites turns into sulphur trioxide gas.
e: Most of the sulphur in copper pyrites turns into sulphur dioxide ($SO_2$) gas.

q: The copper(I) sulphide produced is converted to copper with a final blast of air.
e: Air oxidizes the sulphur in copper(I) sulphide to sulphur dioxide, leaving behind blister copper.

q: The end product, blister copper, is a porous brittle form of copper which is about 98~99.5% pure.
e: Blister copper gets its name from the blisters formed by escaping sulphur dioxide gas.

q: Copper is refined by electrolysis to get at least 99.92% purity.
e: Electrolytic refining is the final step to achieve high-purity copper suitable for electrical applications.

q: Copper is a reddish coloured metal, and a freshly exposed surface has a pinkish-orange colour.
e: This distinctive colour is a key physical property of pure copper.

q: The melting point of copper is 1084°C.
e: Copper has a melting point of 1084°C.

q: Copper can react with non-oxidising acids such as dilute hydrochloric acid.
e: Copper can react with oxidising acids such as concentrated sulphuric acid and both dilute and concentrated nitric acids.

q: The most common reaction product of heated copper and oxygen is copper(I) oxide.
e: The most common reaction product of heated copper and oxygen is copper(II) oxide ($CuO$).
